values.Abstract: Will propose a unified model of Functional Neurological Disorder (FND) that integrates the Free Energy Principle with dynamic systems theory to explain core clinical features such as day-to-day variability and refractoriness. This approach allows us to understand how imbalances in top-down and bottom-up processes create pathological attractor states and provides us novel therapeutic strategies that recalibrate precision weighting in the brain. Using mathematical models and empirical insights, we propose how targeted interventions can help the system escape maladaptive states, paving the way for more adaptive brain dynamics. This framework not only deepens our mechanistic understanding of FND but also raises important questions for future clinical research and treatment development.

values.Title or name of stream: Beyond “not-falling”: A mechano-regulation paradigm for balancing in animals and robots
values.Copypasta:
Theoretical Neurobiology Group  ~ 5/27/2025 at  UTC 
Nick Wilkinson
Beyond “not-falling”: A mechano-regulation paradigm for balancing in animals and robots 
https://youtu.be/vh_LNbv3WjA
values.Newsletter Copypasta: 5/27/2025 - Theoretical Neurobiology Group  https://youtu.be/vh_LNbv3WjA on Beyond “not-falling”: A mechano-regulation paradigm for balancing in animals and robots
values.Abstract: From birth until death animals “instinctively” resist gravity, effortfully asserting bodily form, behaviour, and postural balance. Many basic negentropic tasks are understood as vital homeostasis/allostasis (e.g. thermo-regulation). However balance is taken to be an exception, conceived instead as an ancillary sensorimotor control task and understood intuitively as “not-falling”. In this talk, I’ll question this intuited default framing and defend a more general model of balance as one aspect of a distinct domain of mechano-regulation. I’ll define the underlying biophysical cost function and the core homeostatic set-point/goal, and explain how animals apprehend and embed this goal through a specific developmental process. I’ll outline prospectively how active inference robots of arbitrary morphology could develop a similar “instinct” to resist gravity, and how closed-loop homeostatic feedback could drive learning of sensorimotor control in soft robotics and quasi ∞DoF bodies.

values.Copypasta:

values.Newsletter Copypasta: 6/9/2025 - Theoretical Neurobiology Group  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1Ca5F4wYzVw on Valence-partitioned inference and temporal-difference belief updating for computational psychiatry
values.Abstract: As a an approximate Bayesian, I recently had a bit of a shock. To explain, I will first review persuasive work on the superiority of approximate Bayesian models in describing social neuroscience processes, especially evaluating self and others, and how these models are improved by the incorporation of active inference principles. However, in recent years, deep brain electrochemistry gave evidence for correlates of valence-partitioned prediction errors derived from temporal-difference (TD) models. To meet the challenge of the electrochemical findings, I describe hybrid TD-Bayesian models, which outperform previously successful Bayesian modeling of behaviour. TD-Bayes seems successful, but theoretically it's rather shocking! After all, TD updating is an experience-based, rather than a generative-model based, way for the brain to update representations. Still, I will speculate on how the valence-partitioned architectures involved may elucidate 'black and white thinking' in psychiatric conditions.

values.Title or name of stream: Conditional Symmetry Breaking: From Dissipative Systems to Intelligence
values.Copypasta:
Theoretical Neurobiology Group  ~ 6/16/2025 at  UTC 
Tyler Clark
Conditional Symmetry Breaking: From Dissipative Systems to Intelligence 
https://youtu.be/gosfitTVTX8
values.Newsletter Copypasta: 6/16/2025 - Theoretical Neurobiology Group  https://youtu.be/gosfitTVTX8 on Conditional Symmetry Breaking: From Dissipative Systems to Intelligence
values.Abstract: While non-living dissipative systems like convection cells can form beautiful patterns, they collapse when conditions change because they lack memory—so what allows biological systems to adapt and persist through environmental fluctuations? This work proposes that the key difference lies in "conditional symmetry breaking": biological systems use context-dependent, thermodynamically irreversible transitions that embed historical information directly into their physical structure. Computational simulations demonstrate how adding simple memory and hysteresis to self-organizing systems produces robust pattern recognition, resistance to catastrophic forgetting, and emergent criticality that mirrors neural dynamics. The framework suggests these local irreversible computations provide a concrete physical mechanism for how living systems implement the kind of Bayesian inference described by the Free Energy Principle, potentially explaining everything from why cells differentiate irreversibly to why brains don't forget everything when learning something new.

values.Title or name of stream: The future of ActiveInference.jl: designing for modularity, flexibility, ease-of-use, and breadth of application when making tools for active inference modelling.
values.Copypasta:
Theoretical Neurobiology Group  ~ 6/23/2025 at  UTC 
Jonathan Ehrenreich, Samuel Nehrer
The future of ActiveInference.jl: designing for modularity, flexibility, ease-of-use, and breadth of application when making tools for active inference modelling. 
https://youtu.be/Q6AmKmcov6w
values.Newsletter Copypasta: 6/23/2025 - Theoretical Neurobiology Group  https://youtu.be/Q6AmKmcov6w on The future of ActiveInference.jl: designing for modularity, flexibility, ease-of-use, and breadth of application when making tools for active inference modelling.
values.Abstract: Active inference is an appealing and increasingly popular formal framework for modelling behaviour and belief updating. It is a complex modelling approach that presents a somewhat high technical barrier for researchers in the various fields where it is used. The development of easy-to-use software tools help reduce this barrier and make the approach more broadly usable. This includes the original implementations in MATLAB, the Python package pymdp, and implementations in C and Julia. Here, we present ongoing and planned design choices for the Julia active inference package ActiveInference.jl, in order to receive feedback and further insights from the community. Active inference is used for theoretical modelling, machine learning, and applied cognitive modelling (also called computational phenotyping). A goal of ActiveInference.jl is to accommodate all three of these applications, which would facilitate the translation of advances across fields. We also present our vision for a plug-and-play modular structure that allows combining different types of generative models (beyond the discrete-case POMDP ), different types of variational Bayesian perceptual inference processes and optimization algorithms, and different variations of action-selection processes that exist for active inference, such as sophisticated inference and inductive inference. The modular structure can exploit Julia’s extensive ecosystem for Bayesian inference, optimization, neural network, and differential equations modeling, including Turing.jl, the SciML ecosystem, and RxInfer.jl. The aim of this presentation is to share and discuss our envisioned conceptual and implementational design direction to ensure that the package evolves to be maximally useful within the research, modeling, and machine learning communities it is intended for.

values.Abstract: This talk proposes a theoretical framework that positions art as a neurobiological and cultural mechanism for encoding and transmitting abstracted ‘archetypal’ cognitive-behavioral patterns. Grounded in the free energy principle and hierarchical predictive processing, we argue that aesthetic experience optimizes model updating across perceptual, affective, and semantic neural systems by balancing a critical level of entropy and coherence. Artistic expression, initially emerging as memetic constructs, becomes progressively canalized into archetypes (deep priors that stabilize predictive models across individuals and generations). We further explore how altered states of consciousness, particularly those induced by psychedelics, transiently flatten the brain’s attractor landscape, enabling conscious access to latent archetypal content and facilitating its reintegration through artistic practice.

values.Abstract: Groove is a musical phenomenon that induces the urge to move the body rhythmically, emerging from an optimal balance between predictability and complexity in rhythmic patterns (i.e. syncopation). As part of a narrative review exploring groove as a mechanism for social bonding, I explore how using the Active Inference framework, we conceptualize groove as a tool for shared belief updating and non-verbal communication. Groove fosters interpersonal synchronization, generalized synchrony, a federated "dancefloor" and flow states, supporting social cohesion, emotional resilience, and potentially, collective or individual identity formation. Understanding groove's role extends its applications to music therapy, team building, community interventions, and the development of socially aware music recommendation systems. In this talk, I would like to receive your feedback on the Active Inference Groove framework.

values.Abstract: Surprise lies at the heart of both Predictive Coding and Active Inference frameworks. Despite its conceptual centrality, it is sometimes conflated with novelty, and its multifaceted nature remains underexplored. I believe there may be multiple distinct "flavours" or subtypes of surprise yet to be discovered and/or described. The aim of this seminar is to investigate whether surprise can be systematically decomposed into qualitatively different types, and to examine the extent to which specific brain responses can be reliably associated with each of these types.

values.Abstract: In this talk, I will discuss our recent work on active inference in two of the areas of expertise in our group. In the first one, we show a simple neural circuit capable of self-evidencing using continuous representations and the consequences of different architectural motifs and particular partitions. In the second one, we present a different kind of internal model used for human-robot or robot-robot interaction. We conclude discussing our results in the light of their relations with some areas of physics and ecological psychology, presenting also some ongoing ideas and future work.

values.Copypasta:
Theoretical Neurobiology Group  ~ 7/29/2025 at  UTC 
David Glowacki
Numadelic Virtual Reality: An aesthetic paradigm for design beyond day-to-day phenomenology 
https://youtu.be/7n_ixTSAk5I
values.Newsletter Copypasta: 7/29/2025 - Theoretical Neurobiology Group  https://youtu.be/7n_ixTSAk5I on Numadelic Virtual Reality: An aesthetic paradigm for design beyond day-to-day phenomenology
values.Abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) within psychology and neuroscience research is typically used to construct computational renderings of ‘what things look like’ – i.e., which maintain fidelity to day-to-day perception. In this talk, I will describe how virtual reality (VR) can be used to design experiences beyond day-to-day phenomenology. Specifically, I will describe our work to implement a ’numadelic’ aesthetic within VR, which allows people to visualize their own bodies and the bodies of others as light energy, with diffuse spatial boundaries. Despite their minimal phenomenology, numadelic representations produce a strong sense of presence & immersion, with associated emotional and somatic sensations. Combining numadelic representations with cloud-mounted VR technology enables completely new classes of embodied experience like “coalescence” – e.g., where the bodily representations of multiple people can completely overlap, reliably producing poignant psycho-somatic effects. From the perspective of predictive coding, numadelic representations appear to challenge top-down priors for how people imagine their bodies in relation to others. More broadly, VR approaches like these offer an experimental platform for better understanding various aspects of predictive coding.

values.Newsletter Copypasta: 9/8/2025 - Theoretical Neurobiology Group  https://youtu.be/nnTQ3jfKPxo on Finding a Mathematical Language for Collective Intelligence: A Compositional Framework for Multi-Scale Systems
values.Abstract: As AI systems integrate into human organizations, we're seeing hybrid collective intelligence systems that combine market mechanisms, network effects, and hierarchical coordination simultaneously on the same social substrate. This talk addresses the mathematical challenge of extending active inference to multi-agent systems where different organizational forms operate at multiple scales while shaping each other's evolution over time. I propose using dynamic graph substrates combined with multi-scale coarse-graining to formalize how markets, networks, and hierarchies can emerge as different structural priors over the same Bayesian message-passing system, each optimizing collective free energy under distinct constraints. The framework treats different collective intelligence mechanisms as composable priors over evolving graph topologies where agents minimize prediction error at both individual and collective scales. This approach aims to simulate and predict hybrid human-AI collectives - from AI-augmented democratic processes to algorithmic markets embedded in social networks - extending the Free Energy Principle to collective systems.

values.Abstract: This talk introduces a conceptual framework treating emotion not as a static state but as a dynamic, rhythm-like phenomenon—a “fluid of affective inference.” Drawing inspiration from both quantum theory and complex system dynamics, we propose a model where emotional resonance emerges from interactions between internal predictive flows and external synchrony. While detailed structural and mathematical formulations are currently under patent review, the presentation will focus on the philosophical foundations and potential implications for dynamic emotional memory, affective disruption modeling, and the design of relational AI systems. Our aim is to open an interdisciplinary discussion bridging affective neuroscience, philosophy, and computational cognition.

values.Newsletter Copypasta: 9/16/2025 - Theoretical Neurobiology Group  https://youtu.be/TO4w8yy17Fs on The Hidden Architecture of Intelligence: One Pattern. Everywhere.
values.Abstract: What is the universal pattern behind intelligence: from the first living cells to human societies to the machine minds of the future? Starting with the simple question of how anything persists in a chaotic universe, this talk takes a clear narrative journey from basic physics to the shared architecture that governs all intelligent systems. We will trace how persistence against entropy drives the emergence of boundaries, sensing, learning, and world modelling across scales from the first living cells to human societies and future machine minds. The result is a single, scalable pattern: a framework for understanding how intelligence is structured, why it evolves, and where it is heading. We will conclude by looking ahead, asking what this architecture means for collective intelligence, for the next generation of machines, and for humanity’s own purpose in a world where intelligent systems will likely surpass us.

values.Newsletter Copypasta: 9/23/2025 - Theoretical Neurobiology Group  https://youtu.be/rR2D_C_YDkg on TMS Assisted Psychotherapy - Toward an Interdisciplinary, Personalized Framework
values.Abstract: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) is an FDA-approved, noninvasive therapy for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) and Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) in the United States. For MDD, TMS typically targets the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex using high-frequency pulses across multiple sessions to improve mood and reduce symptoms. TMS works by stimulating nerve cells in brain regions involved in mood regulation, activating frontoparietal networks and promoting neuroplasticity via a range of mechanisms. While TMS is effective for symptom relief, research is ongoing to determine how best to combine it with psychotherapy and related approaches to support more lasting, developmental change. Neuronavigation, which uses brain imaging to personalize TMS targeting, offers potential for tailoring treatments to individual patients and expanding TMS applications to more complex or less standardized clinical presentations. This presentation will overview the current state of TMS for psychiatric applications, discuss the relevant literature on combining TMS with psychotherapy, propose a model for TMS-Assisted Psychotherapy (TAP), and briefly touch upon neuronavigation and emerging approaches using AI to develop protocols and guide targeting, seeking input on development of both TAP and AI assisted targeting using emerging machine learning paradigms, and briefly touch upon additional modalities such as Transcranial Focused Ultrasound Stimulation (tFUS) and Temporal Interference (TI), which allow for non-invasive modulation of deeper brain structures . Overview of TMS-Assisted Psychotherapy: https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/experimentations/202505/tms-assisted-psychotherapy-moving-toward-a-paradigm-shift

values.Abstract: Our talk explores how the human brain predicts syntactic structure during natural language comprehension, based on simultaneous recordings from magnetoencephalography (MEG) and electroencephalography (EEG) as participants listened to continuous speech. Our results show that different word classes, such as nouns and verbs, elicit distinct neural responses, and that anticipatory brain activity indicates sensitivity to upcoming syntactic elements. Additionally, we observe potential parallels between biological and artificial language processing, as words with higher predictability scores from large language models are associated with reduced N400 amplitudes. Questions: 1) We observe anticipatory brain activity before nouns appear in continuous speech. From the perspective of active inference, could this reflect not just passive prediction, but also an active process of preparing or shaping expected input? 2) In our data, the N400 amplitude is smaller for highly predictable words, consistent with reduced semantic surprise. Would you interpret the N400 as a direct reflection of a prediction error signal in semantic processing, or as a downstream process related to integration after prediction fails? 3) In our study, we found that nouns elicit stronger pre-onset neural activity and are more easily predicted by large language models, possibly reflecting syntactic priors in both systems. However, unlike the brain, LLMs operate without sensory grounding or action. From the perspective of active inference, how critical is embodiment or sensory-motor grounding for generating syntactic predictions, and do you see a path toward integrating this into future LLM architectures?

values.Newsletter Copypasta: 9/30/2025 - Theoretical Neurobiology Group  https://youtu.be/r20zmoyq-6o on What is an artifact? Active inference and technology
values.Abstract: The goal of this contribution is to explore how Active Inference and the Free Energy Principle (FEP) can provide conceptual tools to deepen our understanding of the human-machine relationship, socio-technical systems, and, above all, design. My argument unfolds in two interconnected parts. The first part claims that Active Inference and the FEP offer an elegant, parsimonious, and—most importantly—physics-based theoretical framework for justifying the extension of agency to artifacts. This is a crucial issue in both technology studies and design. My argument is as follows: In Active Inference, agency is essentially self-evidencing (Hohwy 2016, Friston 2013)—an emergent property of any system equipped with a Markov blanket. The very existence of a Markov blanket (i.e., a specific partition of states that ensures conditional independence between internal and external states, given the blanket states) entails agency as self-evidencing. This is far from trivial, since a Markov blanket isn’t just a label that can be arbitrarily applied to any system (Beck & Ramstead 2025, Thestrup Waade et al. 2025, Hesp et al. 2019). Therefore, for systems with a Markov blanket, being a “thing,” acting, and exchanging information in a particular manner are all intrinsically linked. Moreover, this form of agency should be seen as existing on a spectrum: the complexity and temporal depth of self-evidencing depends on the structure of the Markov blanket and the generative models. This gives us a highly flexible and physics-grounded notion of agency—one that can be extended to artifacts, as long as they possess a genuine Markov blanket. Philosophically, this opens up a rich dialogue with Bruno Latour’s Actor-Network Theory and with new materialism (Bennett 20120, Barad 2007, DeLanda 2016). The second part of my argument focuses on the notion of design. If we accept the premises laid out in the first part, then design can be understood as the act of creating and developing new forms of agency—that is, new Markov blankets and generative models. But what does it mean to create a Markov blanket?

values.Abstract: In this presentation, we discuss the foundations and applications of active inference under conditions of limited feedback. We begin by deriving the free-energy principle in the context of dynamical systems and provide an information-geometric interpretation of free-energy minimization on the probability simplex. The connections between free-energy minimization, fundamental limits of feedback control systems, and directed information from observations to latent states are highlighted. Building on this foundation, we present an application to oncology, where cancer treatment is modeled as a constrained decision process. Here, the patient is viewed as a dynamical system, and treatment policies are designed to minimize tumor progression under strict measurement and clinical burden constraints.

CRT was developed to formalize the physics underlying a candidate hypothesis for how behaviorally relevant neuroplastic adaptations can emerge from prolonged cognitive engagement in sensory-rich environments, such as action video games. I will present empirical evidence from multimodal neuroimaging, including structural, functional, and directed connectivity, that inspired CRT, followed by an overview of its formal construction. I will conclude with a discussion of potential interfaces with the Free Energy Principle and outline future directions for testing and theoretical generalization.

values.Abstract: The objective of this research is to investigate the minimal conditions and properties under which generalized cellular automata (GCA) can effectively display adaptive behavior within their environment, while reinforcing the links between machine learning, free energy, chaos theory and self-organization. The proposed setting features a pre-defined perception-action interface, which acts as a Markov blanket between the environment and a GCA with a set of mixing and structural properties. The latter are tuned for the GCA to exhibit adaptive behavior consistent with the Bayesian and energetic interpretation of the free energy principle. Moreover, the emergent behaviour is constrained to satisfy classical RL criteria, for it to (efficiently) converge to an optimal policy, and information theoretic criteria: for the internal states to encode a compressed and meaningful representation of the hidden causes. The research will have a mathematical focus to derive some proofs in this direction, complemented by numerical analysis where needed

values.Abstract: Explorations to characterize the function of the Mitochondrion within the Eukaryotic cell have largely focused on its central role in generating ATP; “the energy currency of life”. Mitochondria are here reconceptualized as utilising sophisticated bio-electromagnetic oscillators, which dynamically stabilize their function and form synchronised oscillatory networks. This proposal outlines a novel framework where mitochondrial cristae act as resonant cavities, electron transport chains (ETCs) function as phase-locked loop (PLL) reference oscillators, and ATP synthases serve as (driven) voltage-controlled oscillators (VCOs) and demodulators. We propose that fundamental biophysical forces – coherent electron flow, self/mutual inductance, gyroscopic dynamics, and Lorentz forces – govern energy transduction, enable active sensing of local environment and spatial attitude, mediate rapid "electronic" switching, and orchestrate precise metabolic control through coupled oscillations with the Krebs cycle.

values.Abstract: In the future, the main benefits of AI will be that it is different than us humans in that it incorporates the many other ways in which more-than-human natural intelligence operates. Unlike biomimicking the neural network of human brains, in this talk we aim at biomimicking forests’ underground “root brain” – a term forgotten until recently and mentioned for the first time by Charles Darwin and his son Francis. We explore which role the “root brain” may play in advancing Nikola Tesla’s prophecy that “when wireless is perfectly applied, the whole Earth will be converted into a huge brain.” Towards this end, we biomimic the salient features (exploration via branching, exploitation via fusing, and embodiment via entreating) of the unique biological agent mycorrhizal networks – the largest living organism on planet Earth – found underground in all forests and show that active inference outperforms generative AI by an order of magnitude. Further, by widening the scope of active inference from biological to psychoactive agents, we show that biomimetic psychoactives induce profound shifts in cognition of the future 6G World Brain by harnessing their “door in the wall” to escape from the dark-room problem.

values.Abstract: This talk will introduce a real-world immediate opportunity for development and deployment of Active Inference: adaptive management and optimisation of complex heterogeneous workloads running on large scale classical HPC infrastructure. It will then re-introduce the concept of probabilistic bits (p-bits), an emerging new hardware concept that may offer huge benefits for Bayesian and Active Inference in relation to the task above. Finally, two open questions will be posed to the audience: (1) How the task described above can be properly formulated as an Active Inference problem and how can humans be incorporated in the loop? values.Abstract: How do interacting brains become a “shared mind”? In this talk, I will present a formal active-inference model of two agents engaged in real-time interaction, where each continuously updates its model of self and other to minimise surprise. Within this framework, affective states emerge from each agent’s inference about its own identity coherence (prediction errors) and the shifting boundary between self and other. To test these ideas empirically, we introduce geometric hyperscanning, a novel approach using network curvature to track moment-by-moment changes in inter-brain connectivity. This method reveals phase transitions in shared neural dynamics (e.g. moments of rupture and re-attunement in mutual understanding). By bridging a formal model with multi-brain data, the work offers new insights into how collective intelligence arises from interpersonal exchange, and it points toward a multi-scale approach to shared cognition across natural and artificial agents.

values.Abstract: This research introduces and validates a new decision-making model based on the Active Inference Framework with the objective of better explaining individual behavioral differences and their neural underpinnings in psychiatric conditions like suicidal risk. To validate the model, we used a probabilistic learning task, analyzing fMRI data from healthy volunteers and behavioral data from a clinical group with Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) and varying levels of suicidal risk. Our results demonstrate that the AIF model outperforms conventional reinforcement learning models in explaining both behavioral choices and correlated brain network activity. Most notably, model parameters related to heightened sensitivity to negative outcomes successfully distinguished high suicidal risk individuals from non-suicidal individuals within the MDD group, highlighting the model's potential clinical utility.

values.Abstract: We propose that experience and memory emerge from structured resonance between excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) population waves in the cerebral cortex, constrained by cortical geometry and organized by subcortical controls. This mechanism of E–I resonance links deep (layer 5-6) excitatory waves, generating limbifugal predictions, with superficial (2-3) inhibitory networks, mediating error-correction on the basis of sensory input in predictive coding formulations of active inference. When the low-frequency (theta) excitatory waves resonate with in-phase (n:m coupled) higher frequency (gamma) inhibitory waves, the resonance reflects shared information and creates transient standing‑wave “write windows” that persist long enough to induce early LTP in the local synaptic network.

values.Title or name of stream: Deep temporal Models of the Translation Process
values.Notes:
Translation Process Research (TPR) investigates how humans produce translations from one language into another. Several methods have been used to gather evidence for the assumed underlying translation processes, including think-aloud, (retrospective) interviews, questionnaires, screen recording, brain image technologies (EEG, fMRI), etc. In our research, we use keyloggers and eyetrackers to collect behavioral data during the translation sessions. The two data streams are synchronized to establish correspondences between the sensory input (reading) and translational action (typing) and analyzed to arrive -- among other things -- at a better understanding of the relations between translation effort and effects, which heavily depend on the translator's expertise, text difficulty, expected translation quality, etc.
Numerous models of the translating mind have been suggested, some of which suggest that multiple, more or less automatized and/or conscious translation processes complement each other during translation production. In this talk I suggest the Free Energy Principle (FEP) and Active Inference (AIF) as a novel framework for analyzing, specifying and modelling deep embedded translation processes and for simulating their interaction within the POMDP framework. I exemplify how translation-behavioral data (keystrokes and gaze data) elicit traces of a deep temporal architecture, in which human translation production is modelled in several temporally embedded and interacting processes that unfold on different timelines. Following FEP/AIF, the deep temporal architecture allows translators to arrive at a steady state of fluent translation production by minimizing the discrepancy between the translator's internal states and the (textual) states in the external translation environment.

values.Title or name of stream: Topological Deep Learning: Graphs, Complexes, Sheaves
values.Notes: Abstract: The multitude of applications where data is attached to spaces with non-Euclidean structure has driven the rise of the field of Geometric Deep Learning (GDL). Nonetheless, from many points of view, geometry does not always provide the right level of abstraction to study all the spaces that commonly emerge in such settings. For instance, graphs, by far the most prevalent type of space in GDL, do not even have a geometrical structure in the strict sense. In this talk, I will explore how we can take a (more general) topological perspective of the field with a focus on understanding and developing Graph Neural Network models.

Title: Unveiling the Quantum Tapestry: A Journey through Physics as Information Processing
Introduction:
Embarking on a voyage into the realm of "Physics as Information Processing," this blog post encapsulates key insights from a groundbreaking course. Delivered by an expert, the course explores the historical evolution of the idea that physics revolves around information processing. We'll delve into the pivotal moments and concepts discussed in the first session to unravel the intricate tapestry of quantum theory.
Understanding the Holographic Principle:
At the heart of this exploration is the Holographic Principle, an ingenious concept proposing a new scientific perspective on systems exchanging finite discrete information. This paradigm envisions encoding information on boundaries and extracting it, fostering a revolutionary approach to understanding physical interactions. The course introduces a novel way of conceptualizing communication between agents, highlighting the topological nature of this new science.
Time and Emergent Phenomena:
Diverging from traditional geometric frameworks, the course unveils a model of space as an emergent phenomenon, transcending assumptions about spacetime. Time, rather than an absolute external abstraction, becomes a subjective measure for communicating agents. The measure of time is elegantly linked to the flow of information across boundaries, emphasizing a departure from classical physics.
Quantum Information Theory and Its Paradigm Shift:
The course introduces Quantum Information Theory, a transformative framework that redefines physics by emphasizing communication between agents instead of classical notions involving forces and collisions. The radical shift in thinking heralds a departure from classical physics, setting the stage for an in-depth exploration of emergent spacetime.
Wheeler's Vision and the New Physics:
Drawing on the insights of physicist John Archibald Wheeler, the course encapsulates his characterization of the "new physics." The absence of reductionism, circular reasoning, laws, continuum, and a spacetime box challenges classical concepts, fostering a vision where spacetime emerges from users' experiences.
Exploring Classical Physics and Beyond:
Navigating through classical physics, the course revisits foundational ideas from luminaries like Ludwig Wittgenstein, Rolf Landauer, and John Archibald Wheeler. The journey through the mid-19th century examines Rudolf Clausius's definition of entropy and Ludwig Boltzmann's revelation that entropy measures our uncertainty about a system's state.
Birth of Quantum Theory:
Fast-forwarding to the early 20th century, the course explores Max Planck's solution to the black-body radiation problem. This pivotal moment unveils the birth of quantum theory, emphasizing the quantization of energy and its intimate connection with entropy.
The Enigma of Wick's Rotation:
Gian Carlo Wick's contribution to understanding the relation between Planck's constant and Boltzmann's constant is explored. The enigmatic concept of Wick's rotation is introduced, challenging our understanding of the role of the imaginary number in quantum theory.
Conclusion and Future Explorations:
As the course unfolds, participants are promised a rich journey through the origin story of these transformative ideas. Future sessions will delve into quantum information theory, semantics, communication theory, and the emergence of spacetime. The course's ultimate destination is the exploration of applications in biology via the Free Energy Principle, paving the way for fascinating intersections between physics and biology.
Embark on this intellectual adventure, as we unravel the quantum tapestry and contemplate the profound implications of "Physics as Information Processing."

Title: The Evolution of Physics: From Gödel to Holography
In the realm of mathematics and physics, the journey from Kurt Gödel's groundbreaking incompleteness theorem to the revolutionary concept of the Holographic Principle has been both complex and transformative. This evolution not only reshaped our understanding of mathematical systems but also paved the way for groundbreaking ideas in computer science and quantum theory.
Gödel's Incompleteness Theorem: A Paradigm Shift
In 1929, Kurt Gödel presented his first incompleteness theorem, asserting that no formal system containing arithmetic could be both consistent and complete. This implied that within any such system, there would always exist true statements that were unprovable or false statements that were provable, shattering the notion that finite operations could exhaustively enumerate facts.
Gödel's proof, surprisingly simple, involved formulating a self-referential sentence within arithmetic, leading to the conclusion that no agent could fully describe itself. This realization had profound implications for both mathematics and psychology, challenging the assumption that finite discrete operations could encompass all knowledge.
Computation and the Revenge of Gödel's Theorem
The implications of Gödel's theorem spurred an exploration of computation by luminaries such as Church and Turing. The idea that computation is a physical process mechanizable in various ways led to the conclusion that there exist questions with no computable answers. Questions like whether an arbitrary program will halt or what function it computes became undecidable, posing challenges to the goal of understanding everything through finite processes.
However, this setback became a catalyst for progress, laying the foundation for practical programming and the development of multilevel architectures, where each layer remains oblivious to the workings above and below it.
Quantum Physics and the Holographic Principle
Physicist Richard Feynman reintroduced Gödel's ideas in the realm of quantum theory, emphasizing the importance of considering all possible processes when analyzing experimental outcomes. This perspective gave rise to the Holographic Principle, formulated by Gerard 't Hooft, suggesting that any system could be thought of as approximately a black hole.
The Holographic Principle asserts that the information about a system is encoded on its boundary, limiting what can be known about the system's interior geometry. This principle revolutionized the understanding of physical systems, emphasizing connectivity and information exchange across boundaries.
Active Inference and the Free Energy Principle
In classical physics, Judea Pearl's Markov blankets and Karl Friston's Active Inference formalism reinforced the idea that systems persist through time by maintaining the integrity of their boundaries. Friston's Free Energy Principle extended this concept, proposing that all systems act as agents, continuously engaging in a scientific process by building models of their environment based on communicative exchanges.
Conclusion: A New Paradigm
The evolution from Gödel's incompleteness theorem to the Holographic Principle and the Free Energy Principle has transformed the landscape of mathematics and physics. These ideas collectively suggest that our perception of the world is a projection, inscribed on our boundaries by a process that remains elusive. The study of physics, once focused on forces and particles, has shifted towards understanding the communication and information exchange between agents—a paradigm shift that opens new avenues for exploring emergent phenomena, spacetime, and the nature of reality itself.

Undecidable questions posed challenges but became a catalyst for progress, laying the foundation for practical programming and multilevel architectures where each layer remains oblivious to those above and below.
Quantum Physics and the Holographic Principle:
Physicist Richard Feynman reintroduced Gödel's ideas in the realm of quantum theory, paving the way for the Holographic Principle formulated by Gerard 't Hooft. This ingenious concept suggests that any system can be considered approximately a black hole, with information encoded on its boundary, revolutionizing our understanding of physical systems.
Active Inference and the Free Energy Principle:
In classical physics, Judea Pearl's Markov blankets and Karl Friston's Active Inference formalism reinforce the idea that systems persist through time by maintaining the integrity of their boundaries. Friston's Free Energy Principle extends this concept, proposing that all systems act as agents, continuously engaging in a scientific process through communicative exchanges.
A New Paradigm:
The evolution from Gödel's incompleteness theorem to the Holographic Principle and the Free Energy Principle has transformed the landscape of mathematics and physics. These ideas collectively suggest that our perception of the world is a projection, inscribed on our boundaries by a process that remains elusive. The study of physics, once focused on forces and particles, has shifted towards understanding the communication and information exchange between agents—a paradigm shift that opens new avenues for exploring emergent phenomena, spacetime, and the nature of reality itself. Embark on this intellectual adventure, and join us as we navigate the quantum tapestry, contemplating the profound implications of "Physics as Information Processing."

values.Notes:
Hello Bijan,

Your recent textbook is very rich and provocative, and we have been detailing the material  in several BookStreams (playlist here). 
We were wondering if you would be interested in attending any discussion session, at the end of each part of the book or end of the background series overall?  We are currently approaching the end of part one, and will be having an open discussion over the material in the next few weeks. 
Please let us know if you have any availability during the week of 1/9 or 1/16 to attend a discussion session if you are interested. Our regularly scheduled time is Tuesday at 8:30 AM Pacific time, but we are flexible if you would like to suggest another two or three slots that may work better for you in those coming weeks (or later as works for you). 

Let us know if you have any ideas/questions, and Thanks for your consideration.

AII

values.Title or name of stream: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Language Understanding: Using an Ontology to Create A Language Model
values.Paper link: n/a
values.Notes:
A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Language Understanding: Using an Ontology
to Create A Language Model

Formal linguistic semantics has a long tradition of using logic as a way
to capture the objective semantics of language.  We know an
interpretation is wrong if apparently consistent sets of sentences yield
a contradiction when a deterministic method is applied.  But creating
those models has been largely limited to academic works in which a
theory is embodied in rules on paper.  Computational models, in
contrast, have had very shallow or approximate interpretations of
semantics.

   In this current work, I describe how to generate a very large set
(1TB or larger) set of language-logic pairs that is then used to train a
neural-network based language model.  Because the sentences are created
synthetically, we can use a representation that can also generate a
consistent logical interpretation of the sentence automatically.
Because this model uses the Suggested Upper Merged Ontology (SUMO), tens
of thousands of concepts are used.  Because SUMO uses a higher order
logic, we can generate sentences far more interesting than can be
captured in simple triples.  We can use quantifiers, modals, epistemic
and teleological operators and arbitrary levels of embedded clauses.
Because SUMO has been mapped to all of the WordNet lexicon, we can also
freely include synonyms for all concepts, if they exist.  This leads to
a data set that can cover a diverse and interesting subset of English.
